User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm single, live in San Diego CA. My employer Desert Sun Logistics paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 3 clients, got $890 interest from Marcus savings account and $480 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Thanks — this is enough to give a clear, practical answer, but one quick clarification before final numbers: when you say “I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019),” do you mean you actually paid $4,800 in interest during tax year 2023, or are those earlier years when the loan was active and you paid interest then? (Only interest paid during 2023 is potentially deductible on your 2023 return.)

Assuming the $4,800 is interest paid in 2023, here’s how things look and what to do.

Summary / bottom line
- You should report the $8,900 of graphic-design income on Schedule C (self-employment). That income (and related expenses) is separate from your W-2 wages.
- Home office: because part of the work was for your self-employment business, you can take a home-office deduction for the space used for that business. The actual-expense method (using your rent proportion) will likely give a larger deduction than the simplified method.
- Business supplies ($780) are deductible on Schedule C.
- Interest ($890) and dividends ($480) are taxable and reported on Form 1040 (Schedule B not required because total < $1,500).
- Student loan interest (if paid in 2023) is an above-the-line deduction up to $2,500 but phases out based on MAGI — with your income it will be reduced (see calculation below).
- Charitable gift $720 is only deductible if you itemize (Schedule A). With the information given, the standard deduction for a single filer (2023 = $13,850) will almost certainly be larger than your itemized deductions, so take the standard deduction.

Key calculations (estimates)
- Home office percentage = 165 sq ft / 850 sq ft = 19.41%.
- Annual rent = $2,100 × 12 = $25,200. Home-office portion (actual-method) = $25,200 × 19.41% ≈ $4,890.
- Schedule C before home office: gross $8,900 − supplies $780 = $8,120.
- Home-office deduction $4,890 is less than $8,120, so allowed; net profit after home office ≈ $3,230.
- Self-employment tax (estimate): net earnings ≈ $3,230 × 0.9235 ≈ $2,984; SE tax ≈ 15.3% × $2,984 ≈ $456. Half of SE tax (≈ $228) is deductible as an adjustment to income.
- AGI estimate = W-2 $84,900 + net self-employment $3,230 − half SE tax $228 ≈ $87,902.
- Student loan interest deduction limit: the maximum is $2,500 but it phases out for single filers with MAGI between $75,000 and $90,000. With AGI ≈ $87,902 you fall in the phaseout, so the allowable student loan interest deduction will be substantially reduced (roughly to about $350 in my estimate given $4,800 paid — but this depends on exact MAGI and the precise IRS phaseout formula).
- Charitable $720: would only reduce taxable income if you itemize; your likely itemized total (from info provided) is far less than the standard deduction $13,850, so choose the standard deduction.

Forms and lines you’ll use
- Form 1040 — your federal return.
- Schedule C (Form 1040) — report the $8,900 self-employment income and the $780 supplies expense. Also report the home-office deduction (line 30) — see next item.
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (use this if you use the actual-expense method). The result from Form 8829 flows to Schedule C.
- Schedule SE — to calculate self-employment tax on your net Schedule C profit.
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments to Income) — to claim the deduction for half the self-employment tax and the student loan interest deduction (if any).
- Form 1040 lines (or Schedule B only if interest + ordinary dividends > $1,500). With your amounts ($890 interest + $480 dividends = $1,370) you do NOT need Schedule B.
- Schedule A only if you choose to itemize (but with the data you gave, standard deduction is better).

Home office: actual vs simplified method
- Simplified method: $5 × home office square footage = $5 × 165 = $825 (max 300 sq ft). No Form 8829 required. Simpler, but gives a smaller deduction in your case.
- Actual-expense method: you apply the business-use percentage (19.41%) to allowable housing expenses (rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, etc.). With rent alone that’s about $4,890 — larger than the simplified amount. Because your business net income is enough to absorb that deduction, the actual method is likely better. Use Form 8829 to compute and transfer to Schedule C.
- Important: The home-office deduction is only for the part of your home used regularly and exclusively for the self-employment business (your graphic-design clients). You cannot use the same home-office deduction for your W-2 employment.

Documentation you should keep
- Receipts and records for rent (rental agreement, canceled checks), utilities if used, renter’s insurance, and a simple floor plan showing total and office sq ft.
- Receipts for the $780 in business supplies.
- 1099-NEC/1099-MISC if you received them from clients; otherwise keep records of payments received.
- 1099-INT (Marcus) and 1099-DIV (Fidelity).
- A written record/receipt for the $720 charitable donation (you said you have it — keep it).
- Statements or records showing student loan interest paid in 2023 (1098-E if provided).

State tax note
- California has different rules and may not conform to all federal adjustments. You’ll report your business income and deductions on your California return as well; state treatment of some adjustments (like the student loan interest above-the-line) may differ. Check California instructions or consult a CA tax preparer if you want state-specific detail.

Practical recommendations / next steps
1. Confirm whether the $4,800 student loan interest was paid in 2023. If it was NOT paid in 2023, it’s not deductible on your 2023 return.
2. Gather W-2, any 1099-NEC or client payment records, 1099-INT and 1099-DIV, rent records, receipts for supplies, and your charity receipt.
3. Use Schedule C to report the $8,900 and expenses. Use Form 8829 and the actual-method home-office deduction (unless you prefer simplified for simplicity).
4. Complete Schedule SE and take half the SE tax as an adjustment on Schedule 1.
5. Take the standard deduction on Form 1040 unless you have other itemizable deductions (state taxes paid, mortgage interest, property taxes, etc.) that were not listed here and would push itemized over $13,850.
6. If you didn’t have estimated tax payments and you expect a tax due because of self-employment income, consider paying estimated taxes next year or adjusting withholding.

If you want, I can:
- Run the numbers again if you confirm whether the $4,800 is 2023 interest and provide your total federal and state tax withholdings from your W-2 — I can give a closer estimate of tax due/refund.
- Draft a checklist email you can send to your tax preparer with the items and figures above.

Which would you like me to do next?
